title: Assyria, the Rod of God's Anger, and the Remnant
summary: The chapter finishes the poem of judgment on Israel with a woe against those who write unjust laws to rob the poor, widows, and orphans. Then God addresses Assyria, the rod of his anger, which he sends to punish his people but which boasts that it conquered by its own strength; God will humble it as easily as a forester cuts down trees. A remnant of Israel will return to the Mighty God and rely on him, and Zion is told not to fear. The chapter ends with Assyria's army marching toward Jerusalem, only to be cut down like a forest.
story: Chapter 9 promised a king from David's line and then began a poem of judgment against Israel. Chapter 10 completes that poem (verses 1-4) and then turns to the great question it raises: if God uses Assyria to punish his people, is Assyria in the right? The answer is no. Assyria is a tool in God's hand, and a tool that boasts against the hand that wields it will be broken. Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, a remnant will return (7:3), becomes a promise here (verses 20-23). The picture of Assyria's forest being felled leads straight into chapter 11, where a shoot grows from the stump of Jesse. God cuts down the proud tree of empire and raises up a small shoot from David's line.
historical:
Assyria dominated the ancient Near East in Isaiah's lifetime. Its kings, including Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727 BC), Shalmaneser V, Sargon II (722 to 705 BC), and Sennacherib (705 to 681 BC), conquered and deported peoples from Mesopotamia to the borders of Egypt. The cities listed in verse 9, Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, and Damascus, were all captured by Assyrian kings between about 740 and 717 BC, and the Assyrian boast imagined here mirrors the language of Assyrian royal inscriptions, which celebrate the king's strength and wisdom and list conquered cities one after another.

Verses 28 to 32 trace an army advancing on Jerusalem from the north through towns in the territory of Benjamin: Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Gibeah, Anathoth, and finally Nob, within sight of Jerusalem. Scholars debate what event this describes, whether the approach of the Aramean and Israelite armies around 734 BC, an Assyrian movement, or a poetic picture of the threat rather than a record of a particular march. Sennacherib's actual invasion in 701 BC came mostly from the southwest, through Lachish. The prophecy of Assyria's sudden humbling (verses 16-19, 33-34) is connected in chapter 37 with the sudden withdrawal of Sennacherib's army from Jerusalem.
cultural:
In the ancient world, laws were written and issued by rulers and officials, and a society's justice depended on the integrity of those who made and applied them. Verse 1 describes legal corruption: using the machinery of law itself to strip the vulnerable. Widows and orphans, who had no male advocate, were the easiest targets.

Assyrian kings presented themselves as chosen by their gods to rule the world and recorded their victories on stone monuments and palace walls. They typically claimed that their success came from their own might and from their gods' favor. Isaiah's image of the axe, saw, rod, and staff (verse 15) punctures this claim with humor: a tool boasting against the one who uses it is absurd. The nest image in verse 14, of gathering eggs from an abandoned nest without a wing fluttering, expresses the ease with which Assyria plundered nations. The references to Midian at the rock of Oreb (verse 26) and to the staff raised over the sea recall Gideon's victory (Judges 7:25) and the exodus, the two great deliverances God had worked in the past.
literary: The chapter is a series of linked oracles. Verses 1 to 4 conclude the refrain poem of 9:8-21 with a woe and the fourth and final use of the refrain in that poem (it first appeared in 5:25). Verses 5 to 19 are a woe against Assyria, containing Assyria's own boasting speeches (verses 8-11 and 13-14) followed by God's response. Verses 20 to 27 are promises to the remnant, each introduced by on that day or therefore. Verses 28 to 34 are a vivid poem of the enemy's advance, written in short, breathless lines with town after town panicking, until the Lord suddenly lops off the branches. Key words bind the chapter: rod and staff are God's instruments against Israel, then against Assyria; the Mighty God (verse 21) recalls the royal title of 9:6; and the felling of the forest sets up the shoot of 11:1.

outline.t: Woe to those who make unjust laws
Assyria, the rod of God's anger, and its boast
A remnant will return to the Mighty God

doctrines.note: God uses Assyria as his rod without approving its motives. The empire intends to destroy and plunder; God intends to discipline his people. His purpose rules over and through human intentions, and he holds the instrument responsible for its pride.
Judgment falls both on Israel for its injustice and on Assyria for its arrogance. God's justice is not partial: the nation he uses to punish others will itself be judged.
The remnant will return and rely on the Lord. Even a decreed destruction leaves room for a people who return, and Zion is told not to fear, because God's anger against it will end.
The image of the axe and the one who swings it is a picture of providence: history's great powers are instruments that God directs, and they cannot boast against him.

words.note: She'ar, remnant, used five times in verses 19 to 22. The word describes what is left after a disaster. In Isaiah it becomes a word of hope: though the people are as numerous as the sand, only a remnant will return, but a remnant will return. It is the first part of the name Shear-jashub (7:3).

Matteh, rod or staff. Assyria is the rod of God's anger (verse 5), but in verse 26 God raises his own staff as he did in Egypt. The same word describes Moses' staff in the exodus. The rod God uses against his people will be replaced by his rod raised for them.

Gibbor, mighty man or warrior, part of the title El Gibbor, Mighty God, in verse 21. This is the same phrase given to the royal child in 9:6, and here it clearly refers to the Lord. The remnant returns to the Mighty God, which links the coming king with God himself.

christ: Paul quotes verses 22 and 23 in Romans 9:27-28 to argue that God's promises to Israel have not failed, because God has always saved a remnant by grace, and that remnant now includes Jews who have believed in Jesus. The humbling of Assyria and the felling of its forest lead directly into chapter 11, where the shoot from Jesse's stump, whom Christians identify with Jesus, rules with justice for the poor, the very people the unjust lawmakers of verses 1 and 2 exploited. The title Mighty God in verse 21 links the child of 9:6 with the Lord himself, which Christians read as part of the Old Testament's witness to who Jesus is. The chapter also illustrates a pattern fulfilled at the cross: God works through human powers who act for their own evil ends, yet he remains just and accomplishes his saving purpose (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28).

hard.q: How can God use Assyria's cruelty as his instrument and then punish Assyria for it?
hard.a: The chapter raises this directly. God sends Assyria against a godless nation (verse 6), yet Assyria's own intention is simply to destroy many nations (verse 7), and God will punish its arrogant heart (verse 12). The Bible's answer is that God's purpose and Assyria's purpose are different even when they work through the same events. God intends just discipline; Assyria intends plunder and domination, and it takes the credit for itself. It is judged for what it intends and for its pride, not for serving God's purposes unknowingly. Theologians have described this as God's providence working through secondary causes without making him the author of their evil. Some readers find this unsatisfying and ask why God would use cruel means at all. The Bible does not fully answer that question here, but it insists that God is not indifferent to the cruelty, that the instrument is held accountable, and that the judgment serves a purpose that ends in a remnant's return. The same pattern appears in Genesis 50:20 and at the cross.

questions: Verse 1 condemns those who use law and policy to harm the vulnerable. Where might structures, not only individuals, need God's judgment and our attention?
Assyria credits its success to its own strength and wisdom. In what ways are people tempted to take credit for what God has given?
The remnant will no longer depend on the one who struck them but will rely on the Lord. What does it look like to shift your reliance from powerful people to God?
